excerpt: When an assault at work is covered by workers' compensation in Georgia and South Carolina, and the connection to employment that decides it.
keyTakeaways: Workplace violence injuries are covered by workers' comp when the violence is connected to employment — customer attacks, criminal acts during work, coworker disputes over work matters, and violence against high-risk workers generally qualify. A worker who deliberately set out to injure someone is barred (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-17; S.C. Code § 42-9-60). Domestic violence at work is generally not covered. Beyond workers' comp, victims can file personal injury lawsuits against attackers and negligent security claims against property owners other than the employer. Report within 30 days in Georgia (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-80) or 90 days in South Carolina (S.C. Code § 42-15-20).

faqs.question: Are injuries from workplace violence covered by workers' comp?
faqs.answer: Yes — if the violence was connected to your employment. Workers' compensation covers injuries that arise out of and in the course of employment. Violence motivated by work disputes, criminal acts during work duties, and attacks on workers in high-risk occupations typically qualify. Violence from purely personal disputes may not.

faqs.question: What if I was the aggressor in a workplace fight?
faqs.answer: It depends on intent, not just who swung first. Georgia bars benefits when the injury grew out of your attempt to injure another (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-17). South Carolina bars them only if you acted with a deliberate intention to injure someone (S.C. Code § 42-9-60) — a spontaneous scuffle over a work matter is not enough, and the employer has to prove it. However, if a work-related argument escalated and you participated but did not start the physical altercation, coverage may still apply.

faqs.question: Is domestic violence at the workplace covered by workers' comp?
faqs.answer: Generally no — an attack by a partner or ex is for reasons personal to you, not your job, and Georgia's statute excludes it expressly (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-1(4)). South Carolina likewise covers an assault only if the nature or setting of the work increased the risk. In Georgia that cuts the other way: because the injury is outside workers' comp, you may be able to sue your employer for negligence if it knew of the threat and failed to protect you, as a Georgia court allowed when an estranged husband shot an employee inside the plant.

faqs.question: Can I sue the person who attacked me at work in addition to filing a workers' comp claim?
faqs.answer: Yes. A workers' comp claim covers your medical bills and lost wages from your employer's insurer. A separate personal injury lawsuit against the attacker can recover pain and suffering, emotional distress, and punitive damages — compensation not available through workers' comp. In Georgia this does not extend to a co-worker who attacked you over a work matter (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-11(a)); South Carolina allows a suit against a co-worker for an intentional attack. You may also have a negligent security claim against a property owner other than your employer.

faqs.question: How do I report a workplace violence injury in Georgia vs. South Carolina?
faqs.answer: In Georgia, report to your employer within 30 days (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-80) and file your claim within 1 year (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82). In South Carolina, report within 90 days (S.C. Code § 42-15-20) and file within 2 years (S.C. Code § 42-15-40). Also file a police report to create an official record of the criminal act.

faqs.question: Does workers' comp cover PTSD from workplace violence?
faqs.answer: It depends on the state. In Georgia, PTSD is covered only when it comes with a physical injury from the same incident — a worker physically hurt in an assault can claim the resulting PTSD, but a worker traumatized by a robbery without physical injury cannot (Southwire Co. v. George; Abernathy v. City of Albany). In South Carolina, PTSD without a physical injury can be covered if you prove with medical evidence that the event was extraordinary and unusual for your particular job (S.C. Code § 42-1-160(B)) — a bar that is hard for police officers and other workers whose jobs already involve violence (Bentley v. Spartanburg County). An attorney can evaluate whether your psychological injuries qualify.
